subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Moon's Surface Features
description: One-minute skill: The Moon's Surface Features.

hook.text: The Moon's surface is covered in craters, dark plains called maria, and bright highlands. Each tells a different story.

buildup.text: The highlands are ancient crust, 4.4 billion years old. The maria are younger lava flows that filled giant impact basins.

discovery.text: The largest basin, South Pole–Aitken, is 2,500 km wide—one of the biggest impact scars in the entire solar system.

twist.text: The near side has many maria; the far side almost none. Thicker far-side crust prevented lava from reaching the surface.

climax.text: Every crater is a record of an ancient impact. The Moon's airless surface preserves them for billions of years.

punchline.text: No air, no erosion. The Moon remembers every hit for billions of years.

quiz.question: Why does the Moon's far side have almost no maria?
options: The crust is thicker there, preventing lava from reaching the surface
The far side was shielded from asteroid impacts by Earth
Solar radiation destroyed the maria on the far side over time

details.summary: The Moon's surface is a record of 4.5 billion years of solar system history. Dark, flat maria (ancient lava plains) fill giant impact basins, while bright, cratered highlands preserve the era of heavy bombardment.
details.whyItMatters: The Moon's surface is the most accessible archive of the solar system's violent early history. Without atmosphere or plate tectonics to erase features, it preserves billions of years of impact and volcanic history.
takeaways: Dark maria are ancient lava plains in impact basins
Bright highlands preserve heavy bombardment craters
No erosion preserves billions of years of geological history

faq.question: Why does the Moon have a 'Man in the Moon' face?
faq.answer: The dark patches forming the pattern are maria — vast plains of solidified basaltic lava that filled enormous impact basins 3-4 billion years ago. The contrast between dark maria and bright highlands creates the face-like pattern.

faq.question: What is the largest impact basin on the Moon?
faq.answer: The South Pole-Aitken Basin on the far side, approximately 2,500 km across and up to 8 km deep — one of the largest impact structures in the solar system. It exposed deep crustal and possibly mantle material. China's Chang'e-4 mission landed inside it in 2019 to study its composition.
